questions.q: What are the eight steps of the story circle, in order?
choices: Setup, Catalyst, Debate, Midpoint, All Is Lost, Finale, Epilogue, Change
You, Need, Go, Search, Find, Take, Return, Change
Weakness, Desire, Opponent, Plan, Battle, Revelation, Return, Change
You, Go, Need, Find, Search, Return, Take, Change
questions.explain: A character in a comfort zone wants something, enters the unfamiliar, adapts, gets it, pays for it, returns, changed.

questions.q: A character gets the promotion they wanted at the halfway point, and nothing bad follows. What does the circle say is missing?
choices: Take: a heavy price for getting what they wanted
Need: a reason to want it
questions.explain: Steps 5 and 6 come as a pair: the win, then its cost.

questions.q: What does the horizontal line across the middle of the circle mark?
choices: The familiar world of order above, the unfamiliar world of chaos below
The A story versus the B story
questions.explain: Every story is a descent below the line and a return.

questions.q: Whose model did Harmon simplify to make the circle?
questions.explain: He boiled the monomyth down to eight steps without the mythological vocabulary.

questions.q: Why has the circle been so useful in television?
choices: It specifies exact page numbers for each act break
It works at any scale, and it lets characters come home each episode while still changing a little
It only applies to single-camera comedies
questions.explain: TV writers can apply it to a season, an episode, a storyline or a scene.

questions.q: A writer's story never leaves its starting world. Which step of the circle is weakest?
questions.explain: Without crossing into the unfamiliar, there's no descent and so nothing to return from.

ideas: Every story is a descent from the familiar world of order into chaos, and a return.
The character gets what they wanted, then pays a heavy price for it.
Eight steps around a circle, small enough to check against every scene, episode and season.
The structure grew out of a monthly screening night where audiences voted on five-minute pilots.
